entities.name: Ponhea Yat
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ponhea Yat, also known by his regnal name Borom Reachea I, stands as a pivotal figure in 15th-century Cambodian history, reigning from approximately 1400 to 1463 CE. His rule marks the official end of the classical Angkorian period and the definitive establishment of Phnom Penh as the new capital of the Khmer kingdom. Faced with relentless Siamese incursions and the gradual decline of Angkor's hydraulic infrastructure, Ponhea Yat orchestrated a strategic relocation, fundamentally reshaping the political and urban geography of Cambodia for centuries to come. His reign is critical for understanding the transition from the vast territorial empire centered at Angkor to the more localized, mercantile-oriented kingdom that would characterize Cambodia's Middle Period.

Following the capture and sacking of Angkor Thom by the Siamese kingdom of Ayutthaya in 1431 CE, Ponhea Yat made the momentous decision to abandon the venerable, yet increasingly vulnerable, capital. He initially established a temporary capital at Tuol Basan before moving further south and east to the confluence of the Mekong, Tonlé Sap, and Bassac rivers. This new site, strategically positioned for riverine trade and defense, was named Krong Chaktomuk, later evolving into modern-day Phnom Penh. Here, he oversaw the construction of significant religious and administrative structures, including Wat Phnom and various royal residences, effectively laying the foundations for a new urban center that would become the enduring heart of the Khmer nation.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ponhea Yat's decision to abandon Angkor and establish Phnom Penh as the new capital fundamentally redirected the course of Cambodian history, ensuring the survival of the Khmer state and shaping its political geography for the next five centuries. This strategic relocation marked a critical transition from the classical Angkorian era to the Middle Period, defining a new economic and cultural focus.
